content: Parents and family caregivers of children with complex needs often face significant challenges in meeting their children’s needs while maintaining the overall functioning of their families. This can lead to reduced well-being and increased psychological distress. Peer support interventions are designed to improve the well-being of these parents and caregivers by providing enhanced social support. Such interventions may take the form of peer mentoring or support groups, which can be led by peers or facilitators. Although these interventions are widely available, their potential benefits and risks remain unclear. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of peer support interventions, compared to usual care or alternative interventions, on psychological and psychosocial outcomes for parents and caregivers of children with complex needs. This included assessing any potential adverse outcomes. The review involved a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, and others, covering studies published up to May 2021. Additional efforts included hand-searching reference lists, consulting key investigators, and seeking unpublished data. Eligible studies included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), cluster RCTs, quasi-RCTs, controlled before-and-after studies, and interrupted time series studies. The population of interest consisted of parents and family caregivers of children with any type of complex needs, with no restrictions on the setting. A total of 22 studies involving 2404 participants were included in the review. Sixteen studies compared peer support interventions to usual care, three studies compared peer support to both usual care and alternative interventions (though only data from the usual care arm were included in the results), and three studies compared peer support to alternative interventions only. The risk of bias across the studies was judged to be moderate to high, particularly for selection, performance, and detection bias. The review analyzed data for seven outcomes when comparing peer support to usual care: 1. Psychological distress: The standardized mean difference (SMD) was -0.10 (95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.32 to 0.11) based on data from eight studies involving 864 participants. 2. Confidence and self-efficacy: The SMD was 0.04 (95% CI: -0.14 to 0.21) based on eight studies with 542 participants. 3. Perception of coping: The SMD was -0.08 (95% CI: -0.38 to 0.21) based on three studies with 293 participants. 4. Quality of life and life satisfaction: The SMD was 0.03 (95% CI: -0.32 to 0.38) based on two studies with 143 participants. 5. Family functioning: The SMD was 0.15 (95% CI: -0.09 to 0.38) based on four studies with 272 participants. 6. Perceived social support: The SMD was 0.31 (95% CI: -0.15 to 0.77) based on four studies with 191 participants. 7. Confidence and skill in navigating medical services: The SMD was 0.05 (95% CI: -0.17 to 0.28) based on four studies with 304 participants. When comparing peer support to alternative interventions, only one pooled effect estimate was possible for psychological distress, with an SMD of 0.2 (95% CI: -0.38 to 0.79) based on two studies with 95 participants. No studies reported on adverse outcomes, such as mood contagion, negative group interactions, or worsened psychological health. Qualitative data indicated that parents and caregivers value peer support interventions and appreciate the emotional support they provide. The review found no clear evidence of benefits or harms associated with peer support interventions for any of the measured outcomes. Comparisons with usual care showed mixed results, with some outcomes showing no difference between intervention and control groups, some showing effects over time for both groups but slightly more for the intervention group, and others showing mixed effects. Comparisons with alternative interventions also showed no significant differences, which could indicate either similar effects or a lack of effect for both interventions. The certainty of the evidence for all outcomes was rated as low to very low, meaning that the true effects of peer support interventions may differ substantially from the findings reported in this review. While parents and caregivers perceive these interventions as valuable, the current evidence does not provide clear support for their effectiveness. Further high-quality research is needed to better understand the potential benefits and risks of peer support interventions for this population.
